notice: Original formative practice, not official past-paper questions. Year 9 bridges towards GCSE; the 2029 school exam-board choices and Latin set texts still require confirmation. Marks are reviewed by you or a teacher and are not automatic GCSE grades.

questions.subject: physics
questions.prompt: A metal block has mass 216 g and dimensions 2.0 cm × 3.0 cm × 4.0 cm. Calculate its density in kg/m³. Show every conversion.
markScheme: Volume = 2 × 3 × 4 = 24 cm³.
Density = 216 ÷ 24 = 9.0 g/cm³.
Correct conversion: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³ (or 0.216 kg and 0.000024 m³).
9000 kg/m³.
questions.markingNote: Credit equivalent correct explanations. Each numbered point earns one mark unless a different allocation is stated. Do not award a contradicted point. For calculations, award valid independent method marks after an arithmetic error; never award the same mark twice.

questions.subject: physics
questions.prompt: Identical cups contain 100 g of water at 80 °C. After 10 min: bare cup 48 °C; wool cover 63 °C; foil cover 57 °C. Identify the best insulator in this test, support your answer numerically, and give two reasons why one trial is insufficient for a general conclusion.

Repeats are needed to assess random variation or anomalous readings.
Material thickness or another specified uncontrolled condition may differ; equal thickness or controlled conditions are needed.

questions.subject: physics
questions.prompt: A stone has mass 60 g. A measuring cylinder reads 40 cm³ before immersion and 60 cm³ after. A trapped air bubble increases the second reading to 64 cm³ in a repeat. Calculate both densities and explain the direction of the error.
markScheme: Correct displaced volume = 20 cm³.
Correct density = 60/20 = 3.0 g/cm³.
With bubble: 60/24 = 2.5 g/cm³.
Bubble makes volume too large, so calculated density is too small.

questions.subject: physics
questions.prompt: Time / min: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8. Temperature / °C: 80, 66, 57, 51, 47. Draw a temperature–time graph on paper. Calculate the mean cooling rate over the first 2 min and explain why cooling slows in a 20 °C room.
markScheme: Axes labelled time/min and temperature/°C, with sensible linear scales.
All five points accurately plotted and joined with a suitable smooth cooling curve.
Initial mean cooling rate = (80 − 66)/2 = 7 °C/min.
Temperature difference from the surroundings decreases, reducing the rate of energy transfer.

questions.subject: physics
questions.prompt: Describe how to determine the density of a small irregular, non-porous stone that sinks in water. Include measurements, precautions, calculation and a reliability check.
markScheme: Measure dry mass using a zeroed balance.
Measure water volume before and after full immersion; subtract to find stone volume.
Read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level.
Remove trapped bubbles and avoid splashing or loss of water.
Calculate density = mass/volume with compatible units.
Repeat volume measurements and compare results; repeat anomalous readings before deciding whether to exclude them.

questions.subject: physics
questions.prompt: Pure ice at −10 °C is heated until it becomes water at 20 °C. Explain what happens to temperature, particle motion and internal energy before, during and after melting.
markScheme: Solid warms towards 0 °C; mean particle kinetic energy increases.
Particles vibrate more vigorously around fixed positions.
At the melting point, temperature stays constant while both phases are present.
Energy during melting increases potential energy as the arrangement changes, rather than mean kinetic energy.
Internal energy increases during the plateau despite constant temperature.
Once all ice melts, water warms and average kinetic energy increases again.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.prompt: Magnesium burns in oxygen. (a) Balance Mg + O₂ → MgO. (b) A 2.40 g sample forms 4.00 g oxide. Calculate the oxygen mass gained. (c) Explain why this does not break conservation of mass.
markScheme: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.
Oxygen mass = 4.00 − 2.40 = 1.60 g.
Oxygen from the air becomes part of the solid.
Total mass of magnesium plus reacting oxygen equals product mass.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.prompt: In one chromatogram, standard A has a spot at 20 mm and standard B at 40 mm. Sample X has spots at 20 mm and 40 mm. The solvent front is 50 mm. What can you infer about X? Give an Rf value for each spot and explain why the identification is not certain.
markScheme: X is a mixture: two spots show at least two components in these conditions.
Lower spot Rf = 20/50 = 0.40.
Upper spot Rf = 40/50 = 0.80.
X is consistent with containing A and B, but other substances can have the same Rf; a second solvent/comparison is needed.

questions.subject: chemistry
questions.prompt: In alpha-particle scattering, most particles passed through thin gold foil, some were deflected and a tiny fraction returned backwards. Explain how these observations challenged the plum-pudding model and supported a nuclear model.
markScheme: Most passing through indicates most atomic volume is empty space.
Deflections indicate a concentrated region that exerts a force.
Positive alpha particles are repelled by a positive nuclear charge.
Rare large deflections imply a very small dense nucleus.
Most mass is concentrated in the nucleus.
A diffuse positive charge in the plum-pudding model would not account for the rare very large deflections.

questions.stimulus:
saevit amor ferri et scelerata insania belli,
ira super: magno veluti cum flamma sonore
virgea suggeritur costis undantis aeni
exsultantque aestu latices, furit intus aquai
fumidus atque alte spumis exuberat amnis,

questions.translation: Desire for the sword and the criminal madness of war rage, and anger above all: just as when a fire of twigs is placed with a great roar beneath the sides of a bubbling bronze vessel, the liquid leaps with heat, and within it a steaming torrent of water rages and overflows high with foam; the water can no longer contain itself, and dark vapour flies into the air.
